artworks.title: Rough Point from the drive
artworks.description: Built in 1887–91 for Frederick W. Vanderbilt by Peabody & Stearns to look like a 16th-century English manor; the Dukes bought it in 1922 and had Horace Trumbauer enlarge it. Doris Duke left it to the Newport Restoration Foundation, and it opened as a museum in 2000.

artworks.title: The Olmsted landscape and arboretum
artworks.description: The grounds were laid out by F.L. & J.C. Olmsted for the Vanderbilts. Hurricane Carol (1954) washed away the Cliff Walk bridge and badly damaged them. In April 2026 Rough Point was accredited as a Level 1 arboretum.

artworks.title: The Great Hall
artworks.description: The first room you enter: NRF calls it a room full of objects that stand for the Duke family’s success and taste. Look for the 17th-century Spanish curiosity cabinet with Bol’s Portrait of a Young Woman above it, and the red damask wingchairs already listed here in the Dukes’ 1925 inventory.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s pages
artworks.placeNote: Room places on the map are approximate: NRF publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: Curiosity cabinet
artworks.medium: Ebony, brass, glass, ivory, semiprecious stones
artworks.description: This intricately decorated chest was originally used to display special personal treasures, such as natural history specimens, gemstones, and small souvenirs from travels. Several years ago, Rough Point curatorial staff were delighted to discover a secret compartment hidden inside, intended for safely storing documents. Doris Duke purchased the chest in Paris in 1965.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page
artworks.placeNote: The room is the one NRF’s collection page gives; its place on the map is approximate.

artworks.title: Wingchairs in the William and Mary style
artworks.medium: Walnut, other woods, silk damask, metallic thread
artworks.description: These red damask wingchairs draw your attention when you enter the Great Hall. Although they have been on display at Rough Point for a century (according to a 1925 inventory of Rough Point, there were four “red damask wing back armchairs” in the Great Hall), they may be much older than that! Recent re-upholstery work revealed some intriguing clues to the history of these objects—and a mystery…
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page
artworks.placeNote: The room is the one NRF’s collection page gives; its place on the map is approximate.

artworks.title: Portrait of a young woman
artworks.description: This is portrait depicts an unknown woman. Although there has been some speculation as to her identity, it is likely that she was one of the models the 17th-century artist Ferdinand Bol regularly used in his work. Ferdinand Bol painted this woman in the mid-17th century—at the time that the Dutch Empire was at its height, thanks to a powerful naval forced and the control of maritime trade. Doris Duke purchased it in (1971) and put it on display in the Great Hall—a room full of other objects representing her family’s success and reflecting her family’s taste in art…
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page
artworks.placeNote: NRF’s page says it is in this room; the room’s place on the map is approximate.

artworks.title: The Stair Hall and grand staircase
artworks.description: Follow the full-length portraits up the grand staircase: a future king (Van Dyck’s Charles, Prince of Wales), a noblewoman, a marchioness, then Nanaline Duke and, beside her, Doris Duke as a girl of eleven. Three of the Scipio tapestries hang here too; there is a stained-glass window on the landing.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s pages

artworks.title: Portrait of Caroline Spencer, Fourth Duchess of Marlborough
artworks.description: Caroline Spencer, the Fourth Duchess of Marlborough, was a powerful woman. In this portrait— by court portrait artist Reynolds—the Duchess wears a sumptuous dress with ermine lining. Doris Duke purchased this portrait from the estate of Matilda Dodge Wilson of Meadowbrook Hall in 1970 and placed it alongside other full-length portraits of British nobles on the grand staircase of Rough Point. And while we don’t know what drew Doris to this painting in particular—it’s interesting that Doris collected and displayed symbols—like this portrait— of strong, powerful women…
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page

artworks.title: Portrait of Charles, Prince of Wales, later Charles II
artworks.description: Portrait of a young Charles, Prince of Wales (1630-1685), in court costume. This is one of two paintings by Van Dyck, the court painter to Charles I that Doris Duke bought for Rough Point in 1963.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page

artworks.title: Portrait of Nanaline Holt Inman Duke
artworks.artist: Sir James Jebusa Shannon (American and British, 1862-1923)
artworks.description: From 1912 to 1957, this grand portrait of Doris Duke’s mother, Nanaline Holt Inman Duke (1871?-1962), hung in the library of the Duke family’s residence in New York City at 1 East 78th Street. It was moved to Newport in the late 1950s when Doris Duke gave the New York house to New York University. Nanaline was born in Macon, Georgia at a time of great change in American society in the years following the Civil War. She grew up in southern culture but spent most of her married life in the north, becoming part of the New York and later Newport social elite…
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page

artworks.title: Portrait of the Marchioness of Wellesley
artworks.description: This painting from the collection of James B. Duke was purchased in 1923 to hang in his home in New York City. It features Hyacinthe Gabrielle Rolan and her two sons, Richard and Henry. The portrait came to Rough Point some time after January 1958.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page

artworks.title: Series of Scipio tapestries
artworks.description: Roman general Scipio Africanus (larger figure in gold armor at the left) was a favorite example of mercy in warfare in Renaissance and Baroque art. During the siege of New Carthage, Scipio returned a beautiful female prisoner (possibly the figure seated at right) to her fiancé. For this generous act he received a ransom (the gold vessels and armor shown here at the left), which he returned to the couple as a wedding present. In return, the families of the couple pledged their allegiance to Rome…
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page
artworks.placeNote: NRF’s page says it is in this room; the room’s place on the map is approximate.

artworks.title: Portrait of Doris Duke at 11 years old
artworks.description: Doris Duke sat for this portrait in 1923, the year that Rough Point was being renovated for the Duke Family by Philadelphia architect Horace Trumbauer. The artist, John Da Costa, had been commissioned around the same time to paint formal portraits of her father, the tobacco and energy tycoon James B. Duke, and grandfather, Washington Duke, after whom Duke University was renamed in the 1920s.

artworks.title: Tapestry with proclamation scene
artworks.description: One of a pair of early sixteenth-century Flemish tapestries purchased for Rough Point in 1923. When Doris Duke closed and emptied the house of its contents in 1954, these tapestries went to Duke University where they were hung for display in the main Library. They were returned to Rough Point in 1957 and since then have hung at either end of the dining table, which Doris Duke positioned to take full advantage of the ocean views from the eastern facing windows.

artworks.title: Portrait of Charles Oldfield Bowles
artworks.description: Charles Oldfield Bowles (1785-1862) was the son of an amateur painter and musician Oldfield Bowles (1739-1810) of North Aston, Oxfordshire. This was the first of five John Hoppner paintings owned by James B. Duke. He purchased it in 1908 not long after his marriage in 1907 to Nanaline Holt Inman.

artworks.description: The sunroom on the ocean side of the house. The gilded wrought-iron console tables came from the New York mansion where Doris Duke grew up; she moved them here in the late 1950s.

artworks.title: Pair of wrought iron console tables with gilding
artworks.medium: Iron, applied gilt metal ornament, and marble
artworks.description: This pair of tables is in the style of later 18th-century French Louis XVI wall consoles, but they were made in the 19th century to match the scale and opulence of Gilded Age mansions. They were part of the furnishings of the New York mansion where Doris Duke grew up, but moved to Rough Point’s Solarium at Rough Point in the late 1950s.

artworks.title: The Music Room
artworks.description: Part of the Duke family’s 1920s addition, and filled with objects from many cultures. Doris Duke rearranged it many times as its use changed, and in the 1960s hung it with 18th-century Chinese wallpaper she had bought at auction in Paris.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s pages
artworks.placeNote: Room places on the map are approximate: NRF publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: 20 panels of hand painted Chinese wallpaper
artworks.medium: Transparent and opaque mineral pigments on paper
artworks.description: Chinese wallpaper was a popular luxury good made by skilled Chinese artisans for European markets beginning in the mid-18th century. From the late-19th century onwards, American collectors, like Doris Duke, acquired Chinese paper found in the European markets. One of these patterns on the wall of the Music Room was originally installed in Clyne Castle, an 18th century Welsh country house near Swansea. Doris purchased this wallpaper from an auction in Paris between 1958 and 1959 and had it installed in the Music Room sometime in the 1960s.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page
artworks.placeNote: NRF’s page says it is in this room; the room’s place on the map is approximate.

artworks.title: Sunburst wall clock
artworks.description: The Music Room is part of the Duke family addition to the home and is filled with objects reflecting many different design and cultural influences. Doris Duke rearranged this room many times as the use of the room changed. The sunburst clock features a central painted dial with Roman numerals within a beaded frame and sunburst surround. Doris Duke purchased it for the Duke family residence on 5th Avenue in the early 1940s, and it came to Rough Point in the early 1960s.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page

artworks.title: The Kitchen
artworks.description: Late-20th-century appliances sit next to fittings from earlier in the century, including the porcelain-tiled humidor built around 1900 for James B. “Buck” Duke’s cigars.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s pages

artworks.title: Cigar storage case
artworks.description: The Wilke Manufacturing Company also made refrigerators around the turn of the twentieth century that were covered in porcelain tiles, just as on this freestanding cigar case. Unsurprisingly for a tobacco magnate, James Duke owned the deluxe two-door model and likely installed it at Rough Point in the early 1920s when the house was being renovated.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page
artworks.placeNote: Named in this room by NRF’s director of museums (2019); it may have moved since.

artworks.title: The second-floor landing
artworks.description: The two oil studies by Jean-Baptiste Oudry hang here: sketches for panels painted for a French dining room in the 1700s.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s pages
artworks.placeNote: Room places on the map are approximate: NRF publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: Study for decorative panel with two hounds
artworks.description: Two paintings by French artist Oudry hang on the second floor landing at Rough Point are preparatory sketches for paintings commissioned by Samuel Jacques Bernard, the comte de Coubert (1686-1753), for the dining room of his grand hôtel on the rue du Bac in Paris, built between 1740 and 1742. The full-scale paintings were removed in 1887 when the hôtel was dismantled and its decorations sold. They are now in the Museés des arts décoratifs, Strasbourg.
artworks.descriptionKind: From the Newport Restoration Foundation’s Collection page

artworks.title: Study for decorative panel with barbet
artworks.description: This and a second Oudry work of the same size that also hangs on the second floor landing at Rough Point were recently discovered to be preparatory sketches for paintings commissioned by Samuel Jacques Bernard, the comte de Coubert (1686-1753), for the dining room of his grand hôtel on the rue du Bac in Paris, built between 1740 and 1742. The full-scale paintings were removed in 1887 when the hôtel was dismantled and its decorations sold. They are now in the Museés des arts décoratifs, Strasbourg.

artworks.title: Doris Duke’s bedroom
artworks.description: Bright yellow walls (first painted purple), purple curtains and furniture faced with mother-of-pearl, one of her favourite materials. A Renoir of 1875 hangs near an AT&T Merlin phone system of the 1980s: “the place where the 1880s and 90s meet the 1980s and 90s”, as NRF’s director of museums put it.

artworks.title: Jeune fille blonde cousant (Young blonde girl sewing)
artworks.description: Renoir’s painting of a young girl engaged in needlework is the preparatory study for a much larger and more finished portrait. Doris Duke bought it in 1959 at auction from the collection of Thelma Chrysler Foy, another collector and social acquaintance.

artworks.title: Women Designers of the 20th Century
artworks.description: Not just fashion history. Fashioning history. Explore the stories of the innovative, bold, and inspiring women designers featured in the collection of Doris Duke. The exhibit features over 30 examples of the work of innovative and culturally significant designers including Faie Joyce (American, 1903-1988), Tina Leser (American, 1910-1986), Sybil Connolly (Irish [born Wales], 1921–1998), Mary McFadden (American, 1938–2024), Thea Porter (British [born Israel], 1927–2000), and Madame Grès (French, 1903-1993). These women left an indelible impact on the fashion industry and the way we think about ideas of cultural appreciation, conformity, and style…
artworks.descriptionKind: From the exhibition page
artworks.placeNote: NRF does not say which rooms each exhibition uses: the place on the map is approximate.

artworks.title: Fashioning Resiliency
artworks.description: How can we make more sustainable choices with our fashion? Sustainability is something the fashion industry is grappling with after decades of promoting “fast fashion.” Many makers are meeting the challenge of reducing waste by honoring the process of craft and design, focusing on the local, and designing clothing with longevity— and reuse — in mind. Doris Duke’s wardrobe features items that have not only sustainability challenges—materials that were innovative in the mid-20th century now have long-term conservation dilemmas. Her clothing also reflects her connection to the ocean and the importance of place…
artworks.descriptionKind: From the exhibition page
artworks.placeNote: NRF does not say which rooms each exhibition uses: the place on the map is approximate.

artworks.title: Keeping Rough Point Above Water
artworks.description: 130+ Years of Resilience in a Changing Climate Rough Point’s oceanfront location creates dramatic ocean views, but this also comes with some challenges. Saltwater spray, high winds, driving rain, and increasing storms—accelerated by climate change—all have a significant impact. This exhibit will place the challenges of caring for a historic, coastal building and surrounding landscape in context with broader national and global events—including research and messaging on global warming, energy crises, and conversations about historic preservation…
artworks.descriptionKind: From the exhibition page
artworks.placeNote: NRF does not say which rooms each exhibition uses: the place on the map is approximate.

artworks.description: The Newport Restoration Foundation Reflects on the American Revolution In commemoration of the 250th Anniversary of the founding of the United States, this exhibition looks at the period of the formation of the American nation and sense of identity through the lens of objects, stories, and houses in NRF’s collection and tell the story of the founding of NRF on the eve of the American Bicentennial. 1776|2026 reflects on NRF’s role in shaping the way we understand Newport’s colonial past and invites contemplation of the next 50 years…

artworks.title: Newport Galleries
artworks.description: Explore extraordinary examples of 18th-century Newport furniture and decorative arts, discover what makes Newport furniture so distinctive, and make connections between 18th-century decorative arts and current conversations surrounding globalism, cross-cultural exchange, and lived experiences. These gallery spaces feature special exhibitions that take a closer look art, design, and craft.
